chart.how_read: Opened the IPA's chart landing page (revision history, licence, attribution form). Downloaded the full IPA_Kiel.pdf but could not extract its text (no PDF renderer available, the fetch tool declined to transcribe it). Read the official 600 ppi PNG of the non-pulmonic box (IPA_Kiel_CnP_0600.png) as an image: it shows three columns. Clicks: ʘ Bilabial, ǀ Dental, ǃ (Post)alveolar, ǂ Palatoalveolar, ǁ Alveolar lateral. Voiced implosives: ɓ Bilabial, ɗ Dental/alveolar, ʄ Palatal, ɠ Velar, ʛ Uvular. Ejectives: the ejective mark ʼ followed by 'Examples:' p’ Bilabial, t’ Dental/alveolar, k’ Velar, s’ Alveolar fricative. Footer: '© 2026 IPA … IPA Chart revised to 2015/2005; Typefaces: Doulos SIL (metatext); Doulos SIL, IPA Kiel, IPA LS Uni (symbols)'. Codepoints and character names were checked against the Unicode 18.0.0 NamesList.txt downloaded from unicode.org.

count_explanation: The box prints 11 distinct symbols: 5 click letters (ʘ ǀ ǃ ǂ ǁ), 5 voiced implosive letters (ɓ ɗ ʄ ɠ ʛ) and 1 ejective mark (ʼ, printed on its own at the head of the Ejectives column). The Ejectives column also prints four example combinations, p’ (Bilabial), t’ (Dental/alveolar), k’ (Velar) and s’ (Alveolar fricative), under the heading 'Examples:'. Each of these is a pulmonic-chart letter plus the same ejective mark, so following the brief's rule that example combinations are not entries, they are NOT counted; they are recorded in the chart_example and notes of the ʼ entry. There are no shaded or empty cells in this box. Arguable membership: (1) ʼ is a modifier letter that also behaves like a diacritic; the diacritics helper might also list it, but the chart prints it here and not in the Diacritics table, so it belongs to this section. (2) Wikipedia's 'International Phonetic Alphabet chart' shows an expanded non-pulmonic table (ᶑ, voiceless implosives, many ejective affricates and fricatives, click combinations with k/q/ɡ/ɢ/ŋ/ɴ, ʞ); none of those are printed on the official chart and none are counted.

symbols.articulatory: bilabial click (chart label: Bilabial); the letter gives the front (lip) closure only; the rear closure and its accompaniment (voiceless, voiced, nasal, aspirated...) need another letter

features.voicing: not specified by the letter (set by the accompaniment)
features.place: bilabial (front closure); rear closure velar or uvular

acoustic_correlates.text: a transient: a short, sharp release burst produced when the rarefied pocket of air between the lips and the tongue-back closure is opened, with no pulmonic aspiration unless the accompaniment adds it
grouped with the 'noisy' (affricated, longer, friction-like) clicks rather than the 'abrupt' ones; a lip-released burst would be expected to have low-frequency (grave) energy

click bursts as a class are louder than pulmonic stop bursts: in Traill's intensity scale for !Xóõ (reproduced in Miller & Shah) the click bursts rank above pulmonic t, k, q; Ladefoged & Traill (cited there) report click peaks often more than twice the peak-to-peak amplitude of the following vowel onset (about 6 dB)
low-frequency emphasis of the burst (grave) is expected from the lip release; no fetched source gave a measured spectral value for this click

symbols.notes: Chart column 'Clicks', row 'Bilabial'. The name 'bull's eye' is from Wikipedia's 'Naming conventions of the International Phonetic Alphabet', not verified against the Handbook. Confusables listed by Unicode: U+2299 CIRCLED DOT OPERATOR, U+A668 CYRILLIC CAPITAL LETTER MONOCULAR O; ʘ is a non-casing letter. Miller & Shah 2009 had no bilabial click data (the language lacks it).

symbols.articulatory: dental click (chart label: Dental); laminal tongue-tip/blade front closure at the teeth, released with friction; rear closure set by the accompaniment

features.voicing: not specified by the letter (set by the accompaniment)
features.place: dental (front closure); rear closure velar or uvular

acoustic_correlates.text: noisy (fricated) release: a longer burst and a longer rise time to peak amplitude than the alveolar and palatal clicks
the weakest burst of the four coronal clicks relative to the following vowel in Mangetti Dune !Xung

highest spectral centre of gravity of the coronal clicks: about 4000 Hz for female and about 3000 Hz for male speakers of Mangetti Dune !Xung (three of four speakers), reflecting the small lingual cavity

symbols.notes: Chart column 'Clicks', row 'Dental'. Must not be encoded as U+007C VERTICAL LINE, U+2223 DIVIDES or U+002F SOLIDUS (Unicode lists these as confusables); U+007C is the IPA minor-group mark in the Suprasegmentals box, a different symbol. Unicode: 'c' in Zulu orthography. Name 'pipe' from the Wikipedia naming-conventions page.

symbols.articulatory: (post)alveolar click (chart label: (Post)alveolar); apical front closure behind the teeth, released abruptly; rear closure set by the accompaniment

features.voicing: not specified by the letter (set by the accompaniment)
features.place: (post)alveolar (front closure); rear closure velar or uvular

acoustic_correlates.text: abrupt (sharp) release: a short, loud, pop-like transient with a fast rise to peak amplitude
lowest spectral centre of gravity of the coronal clicks, around 1000 Hz for all four Mangetti Dune !Xung speakers, reflecting the large lingual cavity
among the most intense click bursts; click peaks are often more than twice the peak-to-peak amplitude of the following vowel onset (about 6 dB), per Ladefoged & Traill as cited by Miller & Shah

symbols.notes: Chart column 'Clicks', row '(Post)alveolar'. Unicode trap: the character name says RETROFLEX CLICK but Unicode's own annotation says '(post)alveolar click (IPA)'; its 1.0 name was LATIN LETTER EXCLAMATION MARK. Must not be encoded as U+0021 EXCLAMATION MARK. Unicode: 'q' in Zulu orthography. East African alveolar clicks are often flapped (Wikipedia). Name 'exclamation mark' from the Wikipedia naming-conventions page (the Handbook form may be 'exclamation point'; not verified).

symbols.articulatory: palatoalveolar click (chart label: Palatoalveolar; often called the palatal click); laminal front closure from the alveolar ridge to the hard palate, released fairly abruptly; rear closure set by the accompaniment

features.voicing: not specified by the letter (set by the accompaniment)
features.place: palatoalveolar (front closure); rear closure velar or uvular

acoustic_correlates.text: abrupt (sharp) release class, but burst duration varies between speakers: for some it is about half that of the alveolar click, for others similar, which the authors attribute to differences in release dynamics
relatively high spectral centre of gravity: about 2500-3000 Hz for female and 1500-2000 Hz for male Mangetti Dune !Xung speakers, second to the dental click

symbols.notes: Chart column 'Clicks', row 'Palatoalveolar'. Unicode trap: the character name says ALVEOLAR CLICK but Unicode's annotation says 'palatoalveolar click (IPA)'; alias 'double-barred pipe'. Must not be encoded as U+2260 NOT EQUAL TO or U+29E7 THERMODYNAMIC. No name for it was found on the Wikipedia naming page; 'double-barred pipe' is Unicode's alias and is also the Handbook name as recalled (recalled-unverified).

symbols.articulatory: alveolar lateral click (chart label: Alveolar lateral); front closure at the alveolar ridge released at the side(s) of the tongue; rear closure set by the accompaniment

features.voicing: not specified by the letter (set by the accompaniment)
features.place: alveolar, lateral release (front closure); rear closure velar or uvular

acoustic_correlates.text: noisy (lateral, fricated) release: longer burst and longer rise time than the alveolar and palatal clicks, and lower amplitude
intermediate spectral centre of gravity, around 2000 Hz in Mangetti Dune !Xung

symbols.notes: Chart column 'Clicks', row 'Alveolar lateral'. Must not be encoded as U+2016 DOUBLE VERTICAL LINE (that is the IPA major-group mark in the Suprasegmentals box), two U+007C, or U+2225 PARALLEL TO. Unicode: 'x' in Zulu orthography. Name 'double pipe' from the Wikipedia naming-conventions page.

symbols.unicode_name: LATIN SMALL LETTER B WITH HOOK

features.airstream: glottalic ingressive combined with pulmonic egressive voicing (larynx lowering)

acoustic_correlates.text: voicing throughout the closure, typically strong: the larynx is lowered, timed toward the release, which enlarges the cavity behind the closure and keeps vocal-fold vibration going
weak or no release burst: often no air moves through the opening at release (Hausa); in Sindhi intraoral pressure fell to about -2 to -5 cm H2O and air flowed inward at release
voicing may be aperiodic or creaky (reported for Hausa by Lindau, cited by Nihalani); Sindhi implosives had shorter closures than the plain voiced stop
voicing amplitude tends to rise during the closure (where a plain voiced stop's voicing fades), and the following vowel transitions point to a low F2 locus like [b]

symbols.notes: Chart column 'Voiced implosives', row 'Bilabial'. Unicode annotation: 'implosive bilabial stop'; uppercase Ɓ U+0181. Name 'hook-top b' from the Wikipedia naming-conventions page. Nihalani's aerodynamic data are for this bilabial implosive.

symbols.unicode_name: LATIN SMALL LETTER D WITH HOOK

features.airstream: glottalic ingressive combined with pulmonic egressive voicing (larynx lowering)

acoustic_correlates.text: voicing throughout the closure, maintained by lowering the larynx; the release has little or no burst and often no airflow
voicing during closure can be creaky or aperiodic and varies between speakers and languages
voicing amplitude tends to rise during the closure; vowel transitions point to an alveolar F2 locus (about mid-range) like [d]

symbols.notes: Chart column 'Voiced implosives', row 'Dental/alveolar'. Unicode annotation: 'implosive dental or alveolar stop'; uppercase Ɗ U+018A. Name 'hook-top d' from the Wikipedia naming-conventions page. The retroflex implosive ᶑ (U+1D91) is NOT on the official chart; Wikipedia's expanded chart shows it.

symbols.unicode_name: LATIN SMALL LETTER DOTLESS J WITH STROKE AND HOOK

features.airstream: glottalic ingressive combined with pulmonic egressive voicing (larynx lowering)

acoustic_correlates.text: voicing throughout the closure with larynx lowering; weak or absent release burst
implosives at places further back are harder to keep voiced because the cavity behind the closure is smaller (the airflow for voicing fills the partial vacuum sooner)
vowel transitions with a high F2 locus like [ɟ]; possibly some frication at release as with palatal stops

symbols.notes: Chart column 'Voiced implosives', row 'Palatal'. Unicode annotation: 'implosive palatal stop'; typographically based on ɟ U+025F, not on ʃ U+0283 (do not confuse with esh). No name found in a fetched source; the Handbook name is recalled as 'hooktop barred dotless j' (recalled-unverified).

symbols.unicode_name: LATIN SMALL LETTER G WITH HOOK

features.airstream: glottalic ingressive combined with pulmonic egressive voicing (larynx lowering)

acoustic_correlates.text: voicing through the closure with larynx lowering; weak or absent release burst
the small cavity behind a velar closure makes the implosive voicing hard to sustain, so velar implosives are rarer than bilabial and alveolar ones
vowel transitions with the converging F2/F3 'velar pinch' of [ɡ]

symbols.notes: Chart column 'Voiced implosives', row 'Velar'. Unicode annotation: 'implosive velar stop'; uppercase Ɠ U+0193. The base letter is the hook form of g; do not build it from U+0067 plus a combining mark. No name found in a fetched source; Handbook name recalled as 'hooktop g' (recalled-unverified).

symbols.unicode_name: LATIN LETTER SMALL CAPITAL G WITH HOOK

features.airstream: glottalic ingressive combined with pulmonic egressive voicing (larynx lowering)

acoustic_correlates.text: voicing through the closure with larynx lowering; weak or absent release burst; the very small cavity behind a uvular closure makes it the hardest implosive to sustain
vowel transitions like [ɢ]: low F2 and raised F1 near the consonant

symbols.notes: Chart column 'Voiced implosives', row 'Uvular'. Unicode annotation: 'voiced uvular implosive'. A non-casing small-capital letter. No name found in a fetched source; Handbook name recalled as 'small capital hooktop g' (recalled-unverified).

symbols.chart_example: p’ (Bilabial), t’ (Dental/alveolar), k’ (Velar), s’ (Alveolar fricative); correctly encoded pʼ tʼ kʼ sʼ = U+0070 U+02BC, U+0074 U+02BC, U+006B U+02BC, U+0073 U+02BC
symbols.articulatory: ejective: the consonant it follows is made with a glottalic egressive airstream; the glottis is closed and the larynx raised during the oral closure, compressing the air in the mouth and pharynx, which escapes at the oral release

acoustic_correlates.text: on stops: a release burst followed by a gap (the glottal closure is still held) before voicing starts, so voice onset is delayed relative to a plain unaspirated stop but with no aspiration noise; ejectives in Tsova-Tush had shorter VOT than the aspirated stops they contrast with

two typological patterns (Lindau 1984; Kingston 1985, 2005, as summarised by Kye): 'stiff' ejectives with long VOT, intense burst, raised f0 and modal or tense voice at the vowel onset, and fast amplitude rise; 'slack' ejectives with short VOT, ordinary burst, lowered f0, creaky vowel onset and slow amplitude rise; languages and speakers mix these properties
creakier voice quality (lower spectral tilt, H1*-H2*) at the onset of the following vowel and an f0 difference compared with aspirated stops, with marked differences between speakers

often described as 'spat' or popping consonants, but may be weak and easy to mistake for plain stops; on fricatives (the chart's s’) the oral pressure leaks out during the frication, so the ejective quality is less salient

symbols.notes: Printed alone at the head of the chart's Ejectives column, followed by 'Examples:' p’ Bilabial, t’ Dental/alveolar, k’ Velar, s’ Alveolar fricative. The four examples are NOT separate entries (example combinations of pulmonic letters with this mark); their base letters belong to the pulmonic section. The chart's glyph looks like a curly right quotation mark, but the IPA ejective is U+02BC; do not encode it as U+0027 APOSTROPHE or U+2019 RIGHT SINGLE QUOTATION MARK (Unicode notes U+2019 is the preferred punctuation apostrophe and annotates U+02BC 'glottal stop, glottalization, ejective'). IPA number 401 comes from Wikipedia's IPA number page (4nn = segmental diacritic). No official name found in a fetched source; the Handbook name is recalled as 'apostrophe' (recalled-unverified); Unicode alias '= apostrophe'.

problems: The official IPA_Kiel.pdf could not be read as text (no PDF renderer here; the fetch tool would not transcribe it). The section was read from the IPA's official 600 ppi PNG of the non-pulmonic box, viewed as an image; the transcription is mine, from that image.

Wikipedia's 'International Phonetic Alphabet chart' says it shows 'the official IPA chart, revised to 2020' but its non-pulmonic table is an expanded one (ᶑ, voiceless implosives, ejective affricates, click combinations, ʞ). The IPA's own page says the 2020 issue was identical to the 2015/2005 revision, and the current 2026 issue still says 'revised to 2015/2005'. The official box was followed.

Official symbol names (Handbook of the IPA, 1999) could not be checked; the Handbook was not available. ipa_name values come from Wikipedia's naming-conventions page (bull's eye, pipe, exclamation mark, double pipe, hook-top b, hook-top d) and are null for ǂ ʄ ɠ ʛ ʼ; names recalled for those are in notes and tagged recalled-unverified.
IPA numbers come from Wikipedia's 'IPA number' page (a secondary source), not from the Handbook's Appendix 2.

Unicode character names disagree with the IPA labels: U+01C3 is named LATIN LETTER RETROFLEX CLICK but is the IPA (post)alveolar click; U+01C2 is named LATIN LETTER ALVEOLAR CLICK but is the IPA palatoalveolar click (Unicode's own annotations say so). Do not map by Unicode name.
The chart prints the ejective mark with a glyph that looks like a typographic right single quote; the correct character is U+02BC, not U+2019 or U+0027.

Miller & Shah 2009 contradicts itself: the introduction says the dental and palatal click bursts are shorter, while the results and discussion say the dental and lateral bursts are longer than the alveolar and palatal ones. The results/discussion version was used. The click letters in that PDF are in a private font and were identified from context; the order of Traill's intensity scale is therefore only partly certain (only 'click bursts above pulmonic t, k, q' was used).

No fetched source gave acoustic measurements for the bilabial click ʘ, or Hz/ms values for implosives or ejectives (only Nihalani's pressure values in cm H2O). Place-specific formant-transition statements for the implosives and the 'rising voicing amplitude during closure' of implosives are tagged recalled-unverified (the latter appeared only in a search-result snippet, not in a fetched page).
Ejective acoustics vary across languages and speakers (stiff vs slack types, mixed patterns); there is no single acoustic target for ʼ.
Lindau (1984), Kingston (1985, 2005), Ladefoged & Traill (1994) and Traill (1997) are cited only second-hand through the papers that were read.
The Unicode PDF code charts (U0180, U0250, U02B0) were downloaded but could not be read as text; NamesList.txt 18.0.0 was used for codepoints and names instead.
